title: DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim: what young engineers must do to survive AI
excerpt: Google DeepMind's chief AI readiness officer told NDTV that entry-level engineering jobs are drying up as automation takes over routine coding — and the survivors will be the ones who can point to what is irreducibly human in their work.
body:
• The warning: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim told NDTV that entry-level engineering jobs are drying up as AI automates boilerplate code, basic SQL queries, unit tests and debugging — junior software postings have fallen 25% to 55% from their peak years.
  • The India number: About 37% of entry-level tasks in India are now handled or augmented by AI, and fresher/on-campus hiring has been in multi-year decline, according to the June 2026 Cognizant–Pearson study "The AI Workforce Pulse: The Adaptability Imperative."
  • What to do if you're an engineer: Ibrahim's advice is an inward audit — list what you did this month and mark what was irreducibly human: judgment calls, cultural nuance, ambiguous problem-solving. Then deliberately grow that share. Her own path — electrical engineer to Intel's Pentium processor team to DeepMind — is the proof that careers mutate; continuous learning and reskilling are non-negotiable.
  • The hiring signal: She said companies must look for those human skills while hiring, reward them in talent-development strategy, and build them into performance reviews — so make your human contribution visible, not just your code output.

What DeepMind's AI readiness chief said

In an exclusive interview with NDTV CEO and editor-in-chief Rahul Kanwal, Google DeepMind's chief AI readiness officer Lila Ibrahim laid out how young engineers should confront the disruption reshaping their profession. Ibrahim, an electrical engineer by training whose job is to help governments, institutions and societies prepare for increasingly powerful AI systems, framed the challenge as a question every techie should ask themselves.

"What are you doing in your job where it's so very human — you are bringing in your unique skill into that task, into that problem solving."

— Lila Ibrahim, chief AI readiness officer, Google DeepMind

That inward look, she argued, is where survival starts. Most routine tasks can be automated, she said, but a class of work remains that demands human nuance and human understanding of culture and people.

Context & Background

The numbers behind her warning are stark. AI has taken over routine tasks — boilerplate code, basic queries, unit tests, debugging — that once formed the training ground for junior developers. Estimates cited by NDTV put the decline in junior job postings at 25% to 55% since peak years. The pipeline is thinning at exactly the point where careers used to begin.

In India, the picture is sharper still. Roughly 37% of entry-level tasks are now handled or augmented by AI, and traditional fresher hiring — the campus recruitment engine that launched generations of Indian IT careers — has faced multi-year declines, with fresher roles making up only a small fraction of active tech openings. The figures come from "The AI Workforce Pulse: The Adaptability Imperative," a joint global research study released in June 2026 by Cognizant and Pearson.

Impact & Analysis

Ibrahim's advice matters because it comes from the person Google DeepMind has tasked with AI readiness itself — and because it cuts against both panic and complacency. She isn't telling young engineers to abandon the field, nor promising that the old career ladder will return. Her message is that the ladder is being rebuilt around a different axis: tasks machines can do versus work that requires human judgment.

She pointed to hiring as the lever. Companies, she said, should look for these human capabilities while hiring and in their talent-development strategies, and reward them. For engineers, the implication is practical: a track record of ambiguous problems solved, decisions owned, and outcomes delivered now counts more than a résumé of tools the tools themselves write code with.

Her own career is the exhibit. Ibrahim moved from electrical engineering graduate work to Intel's Pentium processor team to the frontier of AI — across eras when each previous skill set was supposed to be obsolete. The lesson she draws is adaptability: so much changed in her lifetime, and the next generation will see the same. Continuous learning, curiosity, and resilience are the durable assets.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The readiness question Ibrahim carries at DeepMind extends beyond individual careers. She has argued that AI literacy needs to begin long before a first job — schools should lean in, teachers should lead students in exploring where AI fits, and students should grow up literate in what the technology is and isn't.

For young engineers watching entry-level doors close, the message is neither reassuring nor hopeless: the jobs are changing faster than the job titles. Those who treat adaptability as a discipline — reskilling continuously, staying close to AI tooling, and cultivating the human judgment machines can't replicate — will define what the next generation of engineering careers looks like.
